speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I as a matter of privilege, but not referring to a report in Hansard, refer to the Montreal Gazette of this morning and ask that there be a correction made in the dispatch entitled:
Sellar urges radical changes in presentation of estimates.
Auditor General critical of officials by-passing spending authority; suggests free food sent overseas needed by workless of Canada.
In the course of the report it is stated that three important briefs were presented by Mr. Sellar to a house committee and then the report continues:
In one of the briefs, Mr. Sellar criticized the principle of gifts of food by the farm prices support and like bodies to organizations in Europe and Palestine which were caring for refugees, especially the undernourished children. Mr. Sellar said that it was surplus food supplies that were given to Europe but he thought that such surpluses should be distributed in Canada if and where real need existed.
I am sure that any member of parliament who read that would be surprised that a public official would be expressing opinions on policy before a parliamentary committee. I immediately got the briefs in question. Although I do not wish to be critical of the gentleman who attempted to summarize them, because they were quite long-as they had to be, because it was necessary for the Auditor General to make reference to the authorities upon which his objective statements were based-I would suggest to him that he read the briefs again. I am sure he will not be able to find, any more than I was able to find, anything that would give the slightest colour to that kind of paragraph.
Civil servants are often taxed with being bureaucrats, but they are in a position where they cannot speak for themselves here, and I suggest that the gentleman who wrote that dispatch when he reads this will in fairness to Mr. Sellar wish to correct the false impression to be derived from the paragraph I have just quoted. I am sure he will do that after he has had time to peruse carefully the briefs he was attempting to summarize.

Indeed his attitude was entirely the reverse, and he was very emphatic about that. subtopic: MAY 23    CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP AND CANADA'S POSITION IN THE COMMONWEALTH

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MAY 23    CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP AND CANADA'S POSITION IN THE COMMONWEALTH
speechtext: I should like to make a brief statement regarding the ceremonies which are being organized for May 23 of this year. As hon. members know, for a number of years May 23 has been observed in most provinces as Empire day.

subtopic: MAY 23    CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP AND CANADA'S POSITION IN THE COMMONWEALTH
speechtext: May 24.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: MAY 23    CANADIAN CITIZENSHIP AND CANADA'S POSITION IN THE COMMONWEALTH
speechtext:
No, May 23. May 24 is
a legal holiday, but on the day before in the schools of many of the provinces there are ceremonies; and the occasion has been described as Empire day. Originally it was-
-a day devoted specially to the study of the history of Canada and to such special other exercises as might tend to increase the interest of the pupils in their own country and strengthen their attachment to the empire to which they belong-
-to quote from the original definition of the purpose of the ceremonies, in 1899. We have received representations from many organizations that some occasion should be provided for emphasizing the advantages and responsibilities of Canadian citizenship in respect of our status and worth in the commonwealth and to the world.
It seemed appropriate that this might be done in the schools in each province on May 23, in such a manner as might be decided upon by the provincial educational authorities, without in any way interfering

with the exercises traditionally observed on that occasion, but rather as supplementing them.
We therefore consulted the provincial premiers and it has been arranged that on May 23 this year the occasion might be found in the schools to give attention to Canadian citizenship as the basis of our position in the commonwealth. It is not intended that it should be a public holiday, but that suitable exercises could be observed, both in schools and by public-spirited organizations, in order that we may become more deeply conscious of our own citizenship and all that it implies.

speechtext: I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs is in a position now to answer the question I brought to his attention yesterday, and which was referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), as to any steps being taken to prevent the recurrence of floods in southern Manitoba.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: SOUTHERN MANITOBA
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED INVESTIGATION BY INTERNATIONAL JOINT COMMISSION
speechtext:
I am in a position now to make a short statement on the question that has been raised by the hon. member for Provencher, and which was raised yesterday by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre.
As hon. members will recall, in a statement to the house on May 3, 1948, the then secretary of state for external affairs replied to a somewhat similar question asked by the hon. member. At that time the minister stated:
Our information is that the present flood . . . did come principally from international waterways which flow from the state of North Dakota into the province of Manitoba. While to some extent it is a recurrent flood, it had caused no disaster of this magnitude since 1916.
That was in 1948.
The reference to the international joint commission, dated January 12, 1948, covering waters from the eastern boundary of the Milk river drainage basin up to and including the drainage basin of the Red river, does allow the commission-
That is, the international joint commission. -to make recommendations with a view to preventing the recurrence of such floods.
The fact that the waters of the Red river have an international aspect, in that they rise in the United States, means that a satisfactory solution of the problem of flood control can be obtained only by the co-operation of the governments of both countries. It was for this reason that both governments agreed

to make a joint reference of the matter to the international joint commission. Under the reference the commission, among other things, is required-
To conduct necessary investigations and to prepare a comprehensive plan or plans of mutual advantage to the two countries for the conservation, control and utilization of the waters under reference in accordance with the recommended apportionment thereof.
Control of flood conditions, combined with improved low water flows on the Red river in Canada, is one of the principal objectives this government hopes to achieve as a result of the reference and its investigations. These engineering investigations are being conducted for the commission by a board of engineers from the federal services of the two countries, working in co-operation with provincial and state engineers.
The unfortunate and unhappy conditions which exist today at and in the vicinity of Emerson, Manitoba, result from the high flows crossing the international boundary from the Red river basin into the states of Minnesota and North Dakota, and to some extent from the Manitoba portion of the tributary Pembina river. Control of these waters through construction of storage reservoirs in the United States has been the subject of study in that country, but it has been stated with authority that complete control by that method is not feasible. Additional United States studies are being conducted on which to base a comprehensive plan and recommendations.
The United States government has made, and is making, large contributions to flood control in the Red river basin in that country. Storage dams have been built, channel enlargement has been made and confining dikes have been built. The dams tend to hold waters back from Manitoba, while the other two methods tend to send it downstream faster. Studies indicate, however, that the net effect of these measures on flood peaks in Manitoba is negligible.
Approximately ten miles downstream from Emerson, the Roseau river enters the Red with waters gathered in Manitoba and Minnesota, while at the city of Winnipeg the Assiniboine river joins the Red, bringing with it the waters of the Souris river, which are also under investigation by the commission looking to complete utilization and control.
The various studies necessary to the comprehensive planning of all the phases of these investigations are involved and difficult. The engineers have, however, already gathered a great deal of data on which to base conclusions. These data are being analysed, and it is hoped that on completion of the studies the two nations will have plans which
Inquiries of the Ministry will include measures for the alleviation of flooding such as is being experienced at present.

subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENTS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT AGENCIES

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENTS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have indicated on more than one occasion, it has been my intention to avail myself of the appropriate opportunity to present a motion which will seek to express the opinion of this house in regard to a thorough inquiry into the organization of government, and the ways and means by which the efficiency of government could be increased, the duplication of services avoided, and a reduction in the over-all cost of government effected.
I believe it is particularly appropriate that such a resolution should be moved while we are still considering the financial affairs of the government as presented to this house. It is for that reason I take advantage of the motion to go into committee of ways and means to discuss this subject. At the conclusion of my remarks I shall present a motion which will set out the purpose which I believe could well be carried into effect, to the advantage of the government, of parliament, and of the people of Canada.
First, I should like to read into the record a letter I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) on April 1:
Dear Mr. Prime Minister:
I wish to place before you a proposal which I believe should be given early consideration. It is prompted by the statements made recently to the members of the Senate by the Auditor General, Mr. Watson Sellar, and the information contained in the report presented to the House of Commons a few days ago upon the organization of the national film board.
The report of the film board and the Mainguy report last year both disclosed a very serious lack of organization. It happens that these are the only

two reports since the war in regard to the organization of any department or agency of government. It is, therefore, significant that in these two cases there was evidence of a serious lack of organization which could only lead to unnecessary expense and costly duplication which interfered with the efficiency of the service rendered.
The statements of Mr. Watson Sellar emphasized the difficulty with which members of parliament are confronted because of the unsatisfactory way in which public accounts are presented and the difficulty of dealing with them effectively under present arrangements. For these and other reasons I think that a royal commission should be appointed immediately to inquire into the organization of the departments "of government as well as the various public agencies under the control of the government. This commission should have the widest powers to inquire into all details of organization and also the relationship between the various departments and government agencies.
In view of the statement of the Minister of Finance last Tuesday that we must expect public expenditures to continue at the present high level, I think that it is essential that every possible step be taken to increase the efficiency of administration and avoid duplication of costs as a result of overlapping or inefficient services, such as those which were disclosed in the Mainguy and film board reports.
Yours sincerely,
George A. Drew
The Prime Minister had left Ottawa at the time this letter was delivered; and on Monday, April 3, I received a letter from the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) informing me that the Prime Minister was away and that this letter would be given consideration upon the return of the Prime Minister after the Easter holidays. That is now four weeks ago; therefore I think it is appropriate that this subject should be brought forward at this time.
In a radio broadcast by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on April 11 there was a reference to the general manner of dealing with public accounts. In that broadcast he used these words:
It may be that the procedure for considering the estimates and for organizing government departments and agencies could be improved, as Mr. Drew suggests. The government is always willing to consider seriously proposals along these lines, and it usually takes the initiative in making changes when they are needed.
We have under consideration the budget, and we have passed from the general consideration of the budget to ways and means. If the government had come to any decision to take the initiative in improving the method of dealing with public accounts, it would seem that the matter would have been dealt with by this time. Although that may not have already been done, it may be that the government will approve the motion I shall subsequently make; I hope it will.

When we come to the reasons for a commission of this kind, first of all I am suggesting that the commission should follow a course similar to that followed by the Hoover commission in the United States. When Mr. Herbert Hoover was appointed as chairman of what was officially described as "the commission on organization of the executive branch of the government", he was directed to conduct an inquiry and to make recommendations along lines somewhat similar to those which I shall propose. That commission was made up of twelve men, but its activities were not in any way limited to those of the twelve men appointed to the commission. As soon as the commission had been set up, Mr. Hoover at once enlisted the services of some three hundred of the best business and constitutional experts in the United States. He sought the assistance of people with training which would qualify them to deal effectively with the various fields of government activity. He organized these experts into twenty-four separate "task forces", as he called them. Those task forces were directed to investigate and to analyse each of the distinct administrative responsibilities of the government and of the various agencies of the government. Not only did those task forces of experts inquire into the various fields of administrative responsibility; with the assistance of the most competent accountants they also made recommendations as to ways in which the accounting, and the presentation of the various estimates of the departments of government, could be improved.
I have outlined the general procedure followed by the Hoover commission, because that commission made comprehensive recommendations, the putting into effect of which it has been estimated could effect a saving up to $5 billion a year in the cost of government in the United States, without reducing a single government service now being given. That commission, which was set up in July, 1947, presented eighteen different reports between January and April of 1949. Already many of these recommendations have been put into effect, at an estimated saving of some billion and a half dollars. But there is still under consideration the further implementation of the remaining recommendations made in those important documents.
The government budget is the statement of the financial affairs of the government and of the country, having regard to activities which are under the administration of the federal authority. I think it can be stated that a government budget should clearly answer one simple question: What is the
1984	HOUSE OF
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry money wanted for? A government accounting system should answer one definite and simple question: What are the taxpayers getting for their money?
The present budget and accounting systems have only very partial answers to these questions. In some cases they give the surface indications of what the answer is; in some cases there is practically no answer at all. For that reason it is not surprising that Mr. Watson Sellar, the Auditor General, appointed to audit the public accounts, should have been recommending now for several years an improvement in the accounting methods, an improvement in the system of presenting estimates to parliament, and a system by which parliament, as the body representative of the people, shall once again be able to assume effective control over the expenditure of public money. That is, in its essence, the recommendation of the Auditor General, who is not a civil servant in the ordinary sense of the word but, as has already been pointed out this afternoon, is the one man answerable to parliament, answerable to the House of Commons, who does not come under ;he ordinary civil service requirements.
I think it can be fairly stated that no individual in the public service of Canada holds a higher reputation for integrity, for knowledge of his responsibilities, and for the impartiality with which he has discharged those responsibilities than does Mr. Watson Sellar, the Auditor General. For that reason it is high time the House of Commons should take notice of his repeated recommendations, and take the one effective course to implement these recommendations in a way which will bring to our assistance highly expert individuals who are neither members of parliament nor members of the civil service of Canada.
There are certain subjects which by their very nature can best be dealt with by committees of the House of Commons, or by joint committees of the House of Commons and the Senate; but I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is one of those tasks for which the organization and appointment of a royal commission is particularly suited. Such a commission could bring to its service men and women from every part of Canada with the highest qualifications in each field of endeavour related in any way to the many activities of government or its agencies.
Whether those who would be called to the service of the state and of the people of Canada in this way would follow precisely the same course as was followed by the commission in the United States would of course

be a matter for decision by the royal commission operating within the terms of reference of the order in council appointing it. But I should hope that such a commission would bring to its assistance, in turn, just as the Hoover commission did, the services of persons who could deal effectively with every aspect of the extremely complex problems of government.
One of the great problems facing every democracy today is to make democratic government the most efficient kind, of government in the world, and also to provide effective measures of supervision over the widely increased activities of government which have resulted from the extended activities of all democratic governments during the last war.
Big government may not necessarily be bad government; but the type of big government which has emerged from this last war in most democracies can be bad government and can be dangerous government, unless it is brought under effective and efficient supervision, and devices for making it responsive and responsible to parliament are devised which are in keeping with its vastly extended services.
The method of supervising estimates and accounts suitable for the simple form of government which existed in the days before the last war, and in still simpler form before the first world war, is not adequate to provide that measure of supervision over the accounts and the spending of government which is in keeping with the basic principle of responsible government to which we adhere. The theory of responsible government which is the very bedrock of our parliamentary democracy is not that government be responsible for everything, but that government be responsible to parliament in the one essential requirement; parliament should be in a position to exercise effective control, with real knowledge of every detail of what the government is doing.
Do not let us be carried away by any suggestion that we alone, of all governmental bodies, can exercise completely flawless administrative responsibility here in Canada. The fact is that there have been only two small windows opened up through which the members of this house and the people of Canada can see something of the actual work of government departments or their agencies. Since the end of the war no single department has been fully under examination by any body of experts authorized to inquire into all its affairs. The only two inquiries which have been conducted were the investigation by the Mainguy commission inio certain limited aspects of our naval administration,

and the inquiry which was conducted into the administration of the national film board by a highly qualified group of business experts. In both those cases the reports indicated conditions which should make every member of parliament think about the necessity for a broader examination. I feel sure there is no naval officer in Canada more deeply steeped in the traditions of the Canadian navy or more affectionately inclined toward all who serve in that particular branch of the service than Admiral Mainguy. Nevertheless we find in that unanimous report presented by Admiral Mainguy and his associates such words as these:
Officers were also assigned to work without special qualification and several important departments were treated as though they were temporarily refuges for temporary misfits, rather than as fields of endeavour for the best available experts.
Admiral Mainguy would have no desire to be critical of any branch of the naval service. But, as a highly competent and highly qualified officer he saw these conditions, upon which he reported; and there were other conditions-many of them-which indicated a type of inefficiency, a lack of supervision, which pointed to the necessity for recurring supervision of activities of this kind, rather than a reflection in any way upon the general qualifications or spirit of the Royal Canadian Navy.
Those who have read the report of business experts who inquired into the activities of the national film board will have been struck by the fact that, no matter what kindly expressions might be directed to those associated with that board, there was a picture of disorganization which could hardly be exceeded in any case one can imagine. There was the description of various parts of the board carrying on their activities without supervision and without relation to the activities of others parts of the board. We find in the report tabled in the house such statements as these:
Budgets have been unrealistic, with the result that actual production costs have borne little relation to the budgeted cost.
And again:
Purchase arrangements have been made and, in a few cases, invoices have actually been received before the purchase requisitions have been submitted to the purchasing agent.
And another quotation:
Budgets have been prepared to cover part of the work only.	.
These and other statements indicate a situation which, I submit, should suggest to every member of the house the desirability of the kind of businesslike examination of the organization and interrelationship of
Public Service

Proposed Inquiry departments and government agencies which is carried out from time to time by any important business which expects to maintain some measure of business efficiency.
One of the things which has emerged, even in these very limited views which have been obtained with respect to a very small part of the immensely complex organization of government, and one of the things in fact which has been positively stated by men associated with agencies of government, is that the ordinary cost accounting methods do not apply. Just a few days ago a senior official of one of the agencies of government argued that you cannot apply ordinary cost accounting principles to a public service. Mr. Speaker, I think that cost accounting, which is the modern safety valve of big business, can be applied to government, and that there should be the same type of supervision of even such simple things as telephone communications, telegraphs, correspondence costs and things of that kind, as may be found in ordinary business.
Immense sums of money go into those items. We had, for instance, one new type of governmental activity which developed during the war. That was the creation of publicity and information services for departments of government for the purpose of maintaining public morale, in certain cases, and also, quite frankly, for purposes of propaganda directed to the general purposes of the war-and sometimes perhaps outside the exclusive purposes of the war. That was a development which came very largely with the last war. The fact that these activities continue was demonstrated clearly in a return given in sessional paper 102B and 102C of April 17 last, in which it was disclosed that departments of the federal government which had information and publicity divisions were employing a total of 366 employees to carry on publicity and information at a cost to the people of Canada of $1,275,508.43.
I notice the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has seen fit-as was very proper, if he thought it should be done-to write a letter to the press expressing his own opinion as to why it was necessary for his department to have sixty-four such employees.

I am answering the question. The minister knows perfectly well the kind of propaganda that is going out all the time. Additional propaganda of that kind goes out to create the impression that the only reason there is any hope of adequate hospital facilities is that a plan has been devised by the dominion government. By all means let this government support the provinces in their responsibility for hospitalization, but let us cease this attempt to create the impression that each of these things is being done by this national department. Certainly there are things to be done by that department. There is the administration of the pure food laws. There is co-operation with the provincial departments in matters of wider concern. There is the question of hospitalization relating to special subjects such as Indians and Eskimos. Doubtless more can be said about that another time.
One of the things I would like to have examined in that department, as in other departments, and something I believe members of parliament generally would like examined, is whether there is not the possibility of a great simplification of these services; whether, in those cases in which the dominion government is giving support to the provincial governments, the whole thing could not

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry be placed under the administration of one government or the other, instead of having those services multiplied right across Canada. The same would apply to such departments as those dealing with lands and forests, mines and activities of that kind.
One reason I am so convinced that a great deal can be accomplished by examining the relationship of those departments is the extent to which co-operation of that kind has saved money in a great number of cases, to my own knowledge. Just to give one example, hundreds of thousands and perhaps millions of dollars were saved to the people of this country through the wholehearted co-operation extended to the provincial governments by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) in the education of the veterans who took technical training of various kinds after the war. In that instance the Minister of Labour discussed with the provincial departments of education ways in which effective training could be given demobilized veterans. Then, following the approval of broad plans for training and education of that kind, every cent of the money was paid over to those departments and to the staff set up for that purpose. I do not think there has been a more efficient operation in the past few years in this country than the training given in that way. Again, I recall that there was a great saving to the people of Canada through effective plans for co-operation in certain aspects of the supervision of our forest wealth.
These were not things that had been going on for years; they were new arrangements that had to be made. Through co-operation and examination of the whole problem on a businesslike basis plans were made under which in certain cases provincial departments of lands and forests mapped the great forest wealth of this country and made those photographs available to the dominion government. On the other hand the Royal Canadian Air Force carried out certain other mapping service under the federal government, and those photographs were made available to the provincial departments. I also recall a number of cases in which savings have been made through very effective co-operation between the dominion Department of Agriculture and the provincial departments. These things can be done and for that reason I think there should be not only an examination of the departments I have mentioned in order to bring about a still higher measure of co-operation and efficiency, but also an examination of all departments and the relationship between them.
[Mr. Drew.1

Now let us take one example of the way parliament is called upon to deal with estimates. Speaking about his own department the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Clax-ton) had this to say on April 25:
Because this is a big operation, I have felt that the Canadian people should have all possible information about what we were doing, and accordingly both in and out of parliament more information has been given on defence than ever before and I believe more than is being given in most other countries.
The very day that this statement was being made over the radio by the Canadian Minister of National Defence, the secretary of defence in Washington was giving the most detailed information to congress about every aspect of their defence, except the ultra-secret information connected with such weapons as the atomic bomb, the hydrogen bomb, and guided missiles. All the rest of the information was made available for anyone to read. As has been said so- often, we recognize now that the core of the defence of freedom rests with the United States. If the nation which is primarily responsible for the defence of freedom can give information to its elected members and the people of the United States, then the Minister of National Defence in Canada can certainly give equally full information to parliament and to the people of Canada.
A body of this kind could make inquiries, and could ascertain which part of the accounts, if any, in this country should be placed under any measures of secrecy. Another important thing that should be inquired into in regard to national defence is how this parliament can carry out effective supervision of the purchases for the Department of National Defence which are made by an agency of government not answerable in the ordinary way to the House of Commons. These are things that can be examined, considered and reported upon by businessmen, accountants and experts in that field.
I have put forward these arguments, Mr. Speaker, in the sincere and earnest hope that it may be the intention of the government to support this proposal. After all it is too much to think that we alone, of all the free peoples, should have avoided entirely these measures of duplication and inefficiency, which are ordinarily the inevitable result of a rapid expansion far beyond the size of the organization which was originally planned within the rules that have been set. We have been told on reliable authority that if the recommendations of the Hoover commission were fully implemented there would be an annual saving to the taxpayers of the United States of $5 billion. Proportionately

that would mean a saving in the neighbourhood of $500 million a year in this country. It may well be that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has some justification for a feeling of confidence that, relatively, we have found more efficient methods than others. I certainly am not conceding that, but it may be so. Even if it is so, it is difficult to believe that we would not find that at least one-fifth, two-fifths, or three-fifths of the same measure of weakness had crept into the organization of services as had crept into the services in the United States in precisely the same general field of activity.
In saying this I wish to point out also, that, as I believe, the civil service would actually welcome an examination into their general affairs, so that they would be assured of working under the greatest efficiency possible. By the very efficiency of that organization, they would be assured of reaching the highest positions based upon their qualifications. After all, there is nothing that contributes so greatly to the efficiency of the civil service as confidence within the civil service itself that the organization is one in which promotion and advancement relates only to efficiency and constant good service to the public whom it serves. I repeat that the people of Canada have reason to be proud of the high standard of the civil service of this country, but the civil servants themselves have indicated quite clearly that they wish to carry on their business under more efficient methods in certain details of their activities than they do today. I think such an examination as this would provide them with an opportunity of making recommendations for greater efficiency within that great permanent branch of the public service.
I have sought, Mr. Speaker, to put forward arguments which I believe support the request for a motion of this kind. I did not bring forward the motion until there had been adequate opportunity for the government to give consideration to these proposals. It is four weeks tomorrow since I made my request by letter. I would point out that if in these comments I have made any remarks of a nature reflecting on one department or another, I have done so only in answer to interjections which were made, and because I do know of certain cases through my own experience where very real savings could be made. Even if we did not have a single concrete example before us, and we have many, I still suggest that merely basing our approach upon the experience of ordinary business we could all agree that the time has come for an examination of
28, 1950	1989
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry this greatly expanded business of the people. We could then be sure at least, if of nothing else, that nothing can be done which is not being done to give to the people of Canada the most efficient government possible.
I emphasize once again that the greatest strength of the democracies in the days, the months and the years ahead will be the strength of the economy of government. It is part of the contribution to the struggle against the forces of evil that we keep the cost of government, and through that the taxation of the people, down to the very lowest point consistent with the services that the people want, and consistent with the maintenance of the efficient supervision of our public affairs. The people will form their impression of democratic government by their conviction that democratic government is either efficient or inefficient. What I have suggested would be the surest way of giving convincing evidence to the people of Canada that we have done all within our power to make democratic government in this country as efficient and as economical as is humanly possible.
I therefore move, Mr. Speaker, seconded by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker):
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Consideration should be given to the matter of appointing a royal commission for the purpose of examining and making recommendations for:
1.	Reducing public expenditure to the lowest point consistent with efficiency.
2.	Eliminating duplication of overlapping servioes.
3.	Consolidating all public services and departmental activities of a similar nature.
4.	Improving the general efficiency of government and assuring to all members of the civil service full recognition of their responsibilities.
And without limiting the generality of the foregoing to make such further recommendations as may contribute to the general efficiency of the organization of government."

I felt that this idea was implied in


his letter, but it was not explicitly stated; and I think it is better for us to know exactly what is in the mind of each of us in this matter, because it is something which is of consequence not only to this day but to the future.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENTS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
As the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has indicated, Mr. Speaker, I had had some thought that, in closing the budget debate, it might be appropriate for me to say something about the suggestions put forward by the leader of the opposition in the letter to which he has referred concerning the appointment of this royal commission to look into the methods of government expenditure and the way in which those expenditures are scrutinized and examined. But the circumstances yesterday evening seemed to be conducive to a speedy disposition of the budget resolutions, and since the hon. gentleman had indicated that he intended to deal with the matter at a later date, I deferred making those remarks.
In a radio broadcast which I made after the receipt of the letter to which he referred and which was touched on by one of the speakers in the budget debate, I indicated that-and I am sure hon. members will agree it is the case-historically, at any rate, it was the primary function of parliament and if I may say so, of the opposition in particular, to perform the duty which my hon. friend is suggesting should be discharged by this so-called Canadian Hoover commission. As someone put it, I challenged the opposition to perform their historical function and to indicate some of the ways expenditures might be reduced and any of the ways efficiency might be improved.
May I say that one or two hon. members of the opposition have already accepted that challenge. The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), in the able speech he made the other day, indicated certain specific fields in which he felt expenditures could be reduced. I am not going to discuss at this time the merits of the particular suggestions which he made. But in that speech lie did demonstrate that he had spent a great deal of time in analysing the estimates as presented, in co-ordinating figures which appear in them and in putting forward specific suggestions.
May I say by way of digression that I have never been too much impressed by the charges that it is not possible to get adequate information in order to intelligently

discuss the estimates. I do not want to single out individuals but there are a number of members in this house-perhaps the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is a notable example-who know how to ask questions in order to get information they want. If in reply to any question the hon. member for Lake Centre does not get an answer that satisfies him he is never backward in asking for supplementary information. That is the proper course to follow. That is the proper function of an opposition.
In his letter my hon. friend has suggested that there exists in the government service waste, extravagance, duplication of services and the like. I categorically challenge that statement; I categorically deny it. In my judgment there is no duplication, waste and extravagance.
As I said in my budget speech, and as I have said in radio broadcasts since, I would be the last to suggest that there is no room for increased efficiency and improvement in the government service, and efforts are being made at all times-with some considerable measure of success, may I say

to increase the efficiency and to eliminate such wasteful practices as may exist, and these efforts will be continued.
Incidentally I was interested in the tribute which the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) paid the other day to the work of the treasury board. And I speak with some knowledge of that because I spend a good deal of my time sitting on that board going into the tiresome, wearisome details of individual departmental expenditures.
The primary reason why the government feels that we would not be justified in accepting the suggestion that we should set up this outside board of accountants, business experts, or what have you, to decide what is, after all, the primary function of parliament, and in particular the function of the opposition, is that it has not yet been demonstrated, in our opinion, that parliament is unable to fulfil that function. We have a good many existing vehicles at hand. Let me note in passing that even in committee of supply on the estimates, in my observation, it has not been the practice of the opposition to ask the minister of the particular department concerned to give details of, let us say, the number of persons who are engaged in so-called informational activities, and to ask him for a break-down of them, ask him what these people are doing. That is what should be done. But in fact hon. members are, perhaps understandably, more interested in making speeches on general topics. That is a general statement. It does not apply to

Again I will not single out individuals, but I know of two or three in the opposition who are extremely persistent, and rightly so, in getting information as to particular functions of government, whether it be the film board, the C.B.C. or whatever it may be.

speechtext:
Yes. My colleague the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will be glad to elaborate on the excellent work which is being done by the information service in his department when his estimates are under discussion. The point I am making is that members of parliament-and members of the opposition in particular-should see that they get that information.
We talk about failure to be able to examine officials of the departments directly. Let me point out to the house that the public accounts committee is a standing committee of this house. It is true that it examines past and not future expenditures; but surely if one is looking for evidences of extravagance, they are not starting in the coming year. If they exist, they existed last year, and there is opportunity in the public accounts committee for any hon. member, and in particular for hon. members of the opposition, to ask that any deputy minister, or any official of any department, be brought before that committee, and to examine him to their heart's content as to the details of the particular services of the department.
It seems to me that before we talk about setting up outside bodies to do the job we should get down to the dreary, tiresome, politically unrewarding job of digging into the details of expenditures instead of making sententious speeches in the house on general questions.
There is not a complete analogy by any means between our system and the United States system of government. I am not too familiar with the details of the report of the Hoover commission. I understand that it conducted its investigations for some considerable time stretching over two or three years, spent a good deal of money, and made certain recommendations. So far as I have been able to ascertain, up to the present time nothing has been done about them. But the point I want to make is that under the United States system, as the house knows, the executive is not responsible to the legislative body. The cabinet system is very much less highly developed than it is in Canada under the British system. I understand that in the

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry course of its two-year investigation tiie Hoover commission found over 1,800 separate and distinct federal government agencies, many of them with overlapping functions, and so on, none of them directly responsible to any department of government.
Historically, of course, under our system every government agency is responsible to parliament through a responsible minister, and, as I said a moment ago, my colleagues and I believe that the public of Canada have the right to expect parliament itself, the members of parliament itself, to exercise a constant and vigilant scrutiny over the conduct of administration, to search for waste and duplication; in other words, to do the job that they sent hon. members here to do. And if I may say so, I think that the members of the opposition, and of the official opposition in particular, have fallen down on that job. They have done a lot of talking about waste and extravagance; they have done a lot of talking about their being unable to get information as to the details of the public service, and they have made a lot of general speeches; but they have not got down to brass tacks in the public accounts committee, or in this house, to scrutinize the details of expenditures in any single government department. Until that is done I do not think that the government, or this parliament, would be justified in hiring some outside body of people, who would not be responsible to anyone but themselves, however capable, however competent they might be, to discharge a function which is historically, and properly so, the function of this House of Commons.

of the presentation of the estimates is concerned, I have a perfectly open mind. We attempted to make some improvements this year by, for instance, consolidating the items, as was suggested by the Auditor General. But let me point out to the house that I have been reluctant to carry that practice too far, because it takes away from parliament a considerable measure of control and gives a very much wider measure of discretion to the executive.
However, as to the form in which the estimates are presented, or as to the detail the house may wish to have, I have a completely open mind. If they wish to have the estimates presented in ten volumes, it is all right with me. When we come to consider the details in treasury board, which is a long operation extending over several months, there is a tremendous mass of detail presented. Personally, I believe very little use would be made of it by most of the members if that detail were printed in extenso in the estimates, and it would run to considerable expense. But it is open to any member, either in committee of supply or elsewhere, to ask for the fullest detail about any particular item.
As I say, I have no preconceived ideas about the form of the estimates. It may be that they can be improved upon. It may be that it would be desirable to set up a special committee of the house-a small committee perhaps-to consider the form of the estimates, and to see whether they could be presented in a way through which it would be easier for members to ascertain just what the details are. But, so far as setting up any outside commission is concerned, to make a general survey of government practice and administration, I state, and I state it frankly that until we have demonstrated that we are completely unable to do the job we were sent here to do, I do npt think we are justified in making any such move.
I do not think there is anything more I need to add. I am glad the question has been raised, because I have been waiting for an opportunity to deal with it. However, I have expressed the considered view of the government, and it is the considered view of the Minister of Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up too much time, but I do feel that the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) is important enough to warrant my saying something on the subject. I have listened to his case with a good deal of interest. To some extent he aroused my concern over the whole question of efficiency-in government.

I listened to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and I think perhaps there was a good deal to be said for the attitude he took. I do believe however that the minister is overlooking a number of very-important facts. In the first place, even if we were to agree that he was right in saying that the function of the opposition is to do exactly what is envisioned in this amendment, it would be physically impossible for them to do it in present circumstances.
I believe the Minister of Finance must be well aware of the tremendous number of responsibilities placed upon every member of the house-and particularly members of the opposition. We serve on committees, and if we are to discharge our responsibilities properly we must do a great deal of work on those committees. We have not staffs, as they have in the United States. As individual members of the house we are not given any allowance to retain staffs. We know that in the United States staffs granted to members can carry on research work and provide material so that members of the congress are not necessarily made slaves in the preparation of that kind of material, and have the time to do something more important.
We have not a great number of members on the opposition side of the house. Even if we were to unite all three parties and organize most carefully the division of responsible business, we still would not have sufficient to deal with the details of investigational work as envisioned in the amendment. I know if I were to get down to what I consider my duty in respect of those things mentioned by the leader of the opposition I would simply have to neglect a great many other things that are most important to the business of government, and leave out entirely political considerations which it seems must follow almost every member in the house.
I cannot see how the minister's contention is tenable at all. I would have to have a great deal more evidence than he has been able to give me that we could do it, even if it were laid down as a definite principle that the responsibility of the opposition is to do exactly what is indicated in this amendment.
I have always favoured any proposal which would enable the people's representatives anywhere and in any party to get at the truth.
It is only when we are in possession of all the truth we can possibly muster that we are able to discharge the responsibility devolving upon us as responsible representatives of the people. As things are carried on in parliament at the present time we cannot, as individual members or as members of party groups, discover all the things we need to
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry know, if we are to do the effective work that the people have every right to expect us to do.
For instance, in my budget contribution made some time ago I proposed the setting up of a commission to investigate those factors operating within our economy which cause the gap between national income on the one hand and gross national production of Canada on the other to persist. In other words this would be a commission to find out exactly what it is and why it is that the total of money supplied all the people is not sufficient to move or to distribute the national production. That in itself is a matter of tremendous importance. I say that until the facts of that situation are fully brought to light we shall not in any way be able to take such action as will put Canada in a position whereby she would be effectively cushioned against depression.
The amendment offered by the leader of the opposition calls for a much more comprehensive investigation than I have proposed. I consider however that his amendment could be broadened sufficiently to include the sort of thing I had in mind. As a matter of fact it was during President Hoover's administration that a commission was set up in the United States to do exactly the thing I have proposed. I do not believe it is in any respect a reflection on the honesty and integrity of members of the government when I say that a great many people in this country feel uneasy about the way in which their money is being spent, and how efficiently or otherwise the mechanisms of government are functioning.
I believe most people are aware of a mushroom growth in government during the war. I know I am. I know I have talked to many hundreds of people who had expressed concern about that mushroom growth. They expected, and had every reason to expect, a considerable reduction in the bureaux, departmental layers, employees and expenditures after the war was over, and during the early post-war period. They have not been made aware of any such reductions as they expected. They hear stories today of overloaded branches of government where employees are supposed to be spending much of their time trying to keep happy with nothing better to do than to knit or write letters home or compose odes to a very dull life or something of the sort.
I have heard such stories myself from employees of departments right here in Ottawa. They may have been just pulling my leg, I do not know; but even if they were the stories are persistent. I do not think I am saying anything other than the absolute truth when I say that the taxpayers, the

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry electors of the country, are entitled to know whether there is any truth in these rumours. What is more important, they are entitled to know what measures have been taken to ensure efficiency in every department of government.
I am quite sure the government want to feel secure in the knowledge that they have an efficient mechanism in every branch of government. I pay them the compliment of saying that I believe they are concerned about it. Because I know they are concerned, then I say that they certainly should welcome such a suggestion as we have put forward. The amendment calls for the reduction of public expenditures to the lowest point consistent with efficiency. That does not mean measly cheese-paring. I would not want that sort of thing myself and I would not support any amendment that would hold the government down to a cheese-paring position. I do not think that is what is envisioned, but I certainly do feel that even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would want to know that in every single department of government there is that type of efficient organization he can depend upon, that there will not be a building up of cushions to fall back on.
I would like to see curves prepared showing expenditures by departments according to the months of the year. I guarantee that if experts were to draw a curve for each department it would reveal to members of this house an increase in expenditures just prior to the end of the fiscal year. Such an upcurve in expenditures in the months just prior to the end of the fiscal year I suggest indicates that the department is doing its level best to spend the maximum amount in order that it can make out a good case for as heavy or heavier appropriations for the following year.
I have seen that done, and sometimes it is done quite cleverly in spite of the fine work of the treasury board. I am satisfied that the treasury board is much too busy and cannot possibly do this work efficiently.

According to these estimates in about twenty-three departments the expenditures are up considerably. The decrease of $66 million in the Department of Finance is, I presume, chiefly due to interest savings, and a large part of the decrease in veterans' affairs is due to the fact that not so much needs to be done for our veterans now as just after the war. The budget indicates that the taxation, both direct and indirect, in 1949-50 is greater by $12 million than it was in 1945-46, the year immediately following the war. Realizing that large "cold war" expenditures must be made, I feel that the people of Canada are asking parliament to do something to remove at least a portion of their load of taxation arising from unjustifiable expenditures.
In 1945-46 direct taxation amounted to $1,453,373,000 and indirect taxation to $821,485,000. I believe it was after that date that the dominion dropped the special taxes on gasoline, amusements and parimutuels. In 1949-50 direct taxation amounts to $1,269,500,000 and indirect taxation to $1,016,500,000. In other words, while Canadians are paying less in direct taxation,

which they feel, they are paying a great deal more in indirect taxation which they do not feel when making the payments.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Their national income is very much higher, too.

subtopic: PROPOSED INQUIRY INTO ORGANIZATION OF DEPARTMENTS AND OTHER GOVERNMENT AGENCIES
speechtext:
The national income is higher. I realize that perfectly well. But the fact remains that Canadians are now paying much more in indirect taxation than they were in 1945-46 immediately after the war, and during the period of rehabilitation incidental to the termination of hostilities.
Canadians know what taxation is. They realize the need to meet the challenge of the cold war. Our expenditures in connection with defence and the preservation of our freedom amount this year to $425 million, with an additional amount of $144 million to cover ships and munitions to be delivered in future years. When one brings such an expenditure down to the family level and realizes that they mean $700 for every average Canadian family and 80 cents out of every dollar paid in income taxation, we must realize that we have a responsibility to reduce unnecessary governmental expenditures, not by doing away with social services but through the application of business principles as they have been applied in British Columbia in the past year, and will be applied in the next year. If we could save even a portion of the percentage of savings that the Hoover commission has been able to recommend in the United States, then such a commission would be a worth-while investment.
Such a commission would not be political, and would do no political harm to anyone. It would recommend where needed the application of business principles. It would not be the assumption by a royal commission of the functions of the opposition or parliament. That was not the result in the United States when the Hoover commission was set up; it has not been the result in British Columbia. It is a simple process of 'bringing up to date the machinery of organization in all departments of government to meet a changing world and to cope with the intricacies and difficulties incident to the complexities of modern government.
I feel that in the suggestion made by the leader of the opposition there is a challenge to the imagination of the Canadian people. I found a most favourable reaction to that suggestion after he had made it. Men and women on the farms and in the factories- and in all walks of life-in view of the minister's statement in the budget speech that there is little hope of any reduction in taxation, are greatly concerned about

Such a commission in Canada would be no abnegation of our parliamentary responsibilities. speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 5, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS IN CHURCHILL AREA
speechtext: Is the hon. member going to speak to his bill?

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS IN CHURCHILL AREA
speechtext:
Not if I can get a vote on it without speaking. This is a fairly simple bill.

Canadian Wheat Board Act All it does is to add the word "Churchill" to two sections of the present wheat board act, in those parts of the act where the words "Port Arthur, Fort William and Vancouver" appear. The legislative effect of the amendment will be to make Churchill a basing point under the wheat board act the same as Port Arthur, Fort William and Vancouver, but the operative or practical effect of the amendment will be to place the growers of wheat in the area adjacent to Churchill in the same position as the growers of wheat who live close to the Vancouver area or to Port Arthur and Fort William and who have the advantage of cheaper freight rates to those ports while the wheat producer in the area adjacent to Churchill has to pay freight rates based on Port Arthur and Fort William.
As I proceed I shall show that this means a considerable difference in the net return to the grower in this area. When a similar bill was before the house last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) stated that if a better price were received for wheat grown in that area as the result of Churchill being made a basing point under the world wheat agreement, he would agree with me that the benefits derived from that better price should be passed on to the growers in that area. I should like to quote from Hansard of October 6, 1949, where I am reported as follows:
The minister did not answer my inquiry as to what the possible price might be at Churchill under the world wheat contract. Possibly he cannot do so at the present time, but if a favourable price is obtained for wheat at the port of Churchill under the world contract, a price in excess of the price at Port Arthur or Fort William, then I think it is doubly necessary that the people adjacent to that port should get some advantage from that price.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENTS TO PRODUCERS IN CHURCHILL AREA
speechtext:
I would agree.
I should like to quote from page 1088 of Hansard of March 24, 1950, where the minister is replying to a question which I had asked the previous day with respect to the price of wheat at Churchill under the world wheat agreement. The minister is reported as having said:
In accordance with this resolution Canada may negotiate and complete sales under the international wheat agreement for Churchill shipment at prices in line with c.i.f. prices at destination as compared with St. Lawrence shipment. If such sales can be made, Canada would secure the advantage of cheaper over-all forwarding costs as the result of using this port. However, if Canada is called upon for wheat at the international wheat agreement maximum price or desires to put wheat at the international wheat agreement minimum price, we can only deliver wheat from Churchill at the Fort W illiam-Port Arthur basic maximum or minimum prices as set out in the agreement.
Canada has not been obliged to put wheat at either the maximum or minimum price under the world wheat agreement. Wheat sold under that agreement has been on the basis

of agreement as between the purchaser and seller, without having to make a demand on the consuming nation or on the selling nation. If this favourable price has been established for wheat at Churchill then in view of his statement last year I think the minister should agree that the price should be passed on to the growers in the area adjacent to Churchill.
I know of no other way in which that can be done than by an amendment to the wheat board act such as I have suggested. If the minister could show me that the advantage obtained through selling wheat through Churchill can be passed on to the growers in that area in any other manner, I would be prepared to withdraw my bill. But unless he can do that I think this amendment is necessary in order to accomplish the purpose of giving the growers in the area adjacent to Churchill the advantage of rates to that port.
When a similar bill was before the house last year one of the objections raised by the minister was that there were approximately 40 million bushels of wheat produced in this favourable freight area, but that in the past there had been only a little over 5 million bushels of wheat actually shipped through Churchill. He said that if the bill passed it would mean that the wheat grown in that area would be paid for at the favourable freight rate to Churchill which would result in the growers in other parts of the western provinces subsidizing the growers in the Churchill freight area.
As a matter of fact that has taken place for years with respect to Vancouver. In a return tabled on October 31, 1949, it is shown that during the years 1939 to 1944 the growers in the area adjacent to Vancouver received a subsidy of a little over $10 million because much of the wheat grown in that area was shipped through Port Arthur and Fort William. Largely because of the war, shipments through Vancouver were curtailed. I never heard any complaint by the wheat growers in other parts of western Canada with respect to that subsidization of grain grown in that particular area. I think we all considered it reasonably fair. Again from 1945 to 1948 growers in the area adjacent to Vancouver were subsidized, though not to the same extent. In 1945 the additional freight paid amounted in round figures to $150,000; in 1946 to $361,000; in 1947 to $686,000 and in 1948 to $396,000.
The wheat board received some compensation in return for this additional freight paid on grain from the Vancouver freight rate area shipped through Port Arthur and Fort William. It did not completely cover

the additional cost, but it did meet a considerable portion of it. My contention is that if today we shipped a certain amount of our wheat through Churchill at a favourable price, that money could be used by the wheat board to make up any deficit that might result from the payment to the growers on the basis of the Churchill freight rates. If this were done it would not place a burden on the growers in any other part of western Canada, but would give the growers in that area the advantage of freight rates to that port. I think that only fair, and a very good reason why at this time we should amend the act as I have suggested.
One other matter with respect to grain going to Churchill, about which something * should be done, is the diversion charge which is at present levied by the grain handling companies on grain going through that port. That charge amounts to one and a half cents per bushel. A good many hon. members may not know what diversion charges are, though I believe that yesterday the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), in speaking of the port of Churchill, gave some information on that subject. This is a charge made on grain which an elevator company ships through a port where it has not a terminal elevator of its own and, as a result, has to turn that grain over to another company or place it in a government elevator. As the only elevators at Churchill are government elevators this means that every bushel of grain shipped to that port must pay that diversion charge of one and a half cents a bushel. Practically every elevator company in western Canada has terminal elevators of its own or leases elevators at Vancouver and Port Arthur-Fort William, and ninety-five per cent of the grain they handle goes into their own terminal elevators so no diversion charges are levied on that grain. It seems very unfair that Churchill should be penalized because of this practice. As a matter of fact the On-to-the-Bay association, in making its representations to the cabinet just a few days ago, had this to say:
We would request that government instructions be issued to the Canadian wheat board for the cancellation of unwarranted diversion charges being made by western grain elevators of 1J to 2 cents per bushel on grain when same is shipped to the port of Churchill.
I should like to give some figures to show the difference in cost between Churchill and other ports. The brief of the Hudson bay route association gives certain figures showing the cost of marketing grain from Saskatoon to Great Britain through various Canadian ports. I shall give the total amounts, and then will ask permission to have the complete figures placed on Hansard.
Canadian Wheat Board Act These are official figures of the Canadian wheat board, and show the cost of moving wheat to Great Britain over various routes. From Saskatoon via Churchill the cost per bushel is 45-949 cents. Via Vancouver it is 59-659 cents. Via lake and rail ex bay ports to f.o.b. St. Lawrence ports the cost is 58-037 cents per bushel. Via all-water to transfer points to f.o.b. St. Lawrence ports the rate is 56-671 cents. That is the cheapest rate on grain coming east. Via lake and rail ex bay ports to Halifax and Saint John the rate is 59-605 cents. So it will be seen that on grain shipped to Great Britain through Churchill from points such as Vancouver the saving is from 12 to 14 cents a bushel. If I have your permission, Mr. Speaker, I would ask that the full details of these charges be placed on Hansard, since I believe they would be of interest to all hon. members.

I want to make one other point. Last year the minister stated that approximately forty million bushels of wheat were grown in the area adjacent to the port of Churchill. I disagreed with him, but now I find that he was more nearly correct than I was. Some forty million bushels of wheat, or a little more, were grown in the freight rate area favourable to Churchill; but I would point out that this favourable freight rate area is in the shape of a fan, spreading out from Hudson Bay junction or The Pas. On the outskirts of that area there is a large area where the difference would be only one-half cent or one cent per hundred, so in that area it would make very little difference to the growers which way their wheat went. My argument is that the wheat grown in the area where the freight rate to Churchill would be a real benefit amounts to only twenty-five million bushels or less. This is the area which would be principally affected. The other fringe area, if I might call it that, would not be nearly so concerned, because the difference in cost to the growers would be very little, whichever way their wheat went.
Last year the wheat board had to get wheat to Churchill in a hurry. They were not able to get all they needed in the favourable freight rate area adjacent to that port,


because much of the wheat had gone to Port Arthur and Fort William. The result was that they had to haul wheat, I am told, from as far away as Maple Creek in Saskatchewan to Churchill in order to load the boats coming there in the early part of the season. So I believe that with a little planning the port of Churchill could be used to a far greater extent than at the present time. There is no need to increase the facilities; at present Churchill has facilities to handle twenty to twenty-five million bushels of wheat, if they were used for the full season of eight weeks during which the port is open. If that time were extended by another two weeks in the early part of the season and another two weeks in the latter part, certainly from twenty to twenty-five million bushels of wheat could be shipped through that port.
In my estimation there is only one reason why it is not shipped, and that is simply the fact that the wheat board and the other agencies which handle wheat have not become accustomed to using that port. The shipping companies have never been in the habit of sending their boats into Churchill, but have always used Montreal, Saint John, or Vancouver. Until the wheat board or the Canadian government encourage shipment through Churchill, that condition is likely to remain. The shipment of grain through that port is not likely to grow. It is for that reason I have moved this amendment to the act. I feel that, if Churchill were named as a basing point, the wheat board then would have a greater incentive to find sales for wheat through Churchill. We would then get a greater use of that port, and I am sure that when the port was first built it was intended to give to that part of western Canada adjacent to it another outlet to the sea. There is no use having it there if we are not going to make use of it. I am urging the government to accept this amendment as the first step towards making greater use of the port of Churchill.

If the route causes the over-all cost of marketing grain to be more expensive, then that expense is charged against the growers of western Canada, and the contributions would come not from the government but from the growers in other areas. Nevertheless, it is the duty of the government to make sure that marketing is done fairly, and that each grower receives the price for his wheat that represents an equitable division of the total proceeds of a crop. Canadian Wheat Board Act moment. My hon. friend will appreciate the fact that the port opens at the end of the crop year. It is usually about the end of July before Churchill is open. For part of the Churchill season it is too early to get deliveries from the current crop, so that for such part of the season the movement must depend upon the carry-over from the old crop. For the latter part of the season the movement through Churchill depends upon the early marketings of the new crop. If there were substantial carry-overs such as we often had in pre-war days, there was no great difficulty. We could move grain into the Saskatoon elevator and have it available for the Churchill movement in any quantities that were required. Arrangements are particularly difficult this year because this year marks the ending of the five-year pool. We all know that the price at which wheat is being marketed this year is the highest permissible under the international wheat agreement. There is every reason why all the wheat possible should be , marketed within the pool period.
We know that all the farmers of western Canada are anxious to have this pool completed promptly so that final distribution of pool funds can be made to the growers. There is therefore great pressure on the wheat board to get all pooled grain to market. To hold wheat simply for the privilege of moving it out through Churchill, when that means an inability to sell under conditions that maintain in the present crop year, is a difficult decision to make. The fact that the wheat board, in spite of these difficult conditions, has moved a record quantity of wheat from the 1948 crop through Churchill and has made a still better record in the crop year 1949, indicates I think that the wheat board has the interests of the port of Churchill at heart.
At the present time wheat is being moved out of the country and into' terminals as rapidly as possible in order to fill overseas commitments. Nevertheless instructions have been issued that any wheat that is tributary to Churchill will not be moved at this time. The board will make an endeavour to hold that wheat for movement through Churchill, but nevertheless if wheat continues to be sold at the present rate and if that wheat is required to fulfil commitments prior to the end of the pool year, that wheat must move by another route in order to get that wheat to market on time. I am frank to admit, Mr. Speaker, that the question of negotiating agreements by law on the floor of this house is a matter of opinion. I think I know something about the history of labour legislation in this country. I have a vivid recollection of the early days of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, which was introduced by the Liberal party of that day, and fashioned by the previous prime minister. Labour organizations generally opposed labour legislation in the form of the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act.
Questions of this kind, of course, have been discussed by the British trade union congress and by the leaders of the British labour movement. That labour movement, I think it is fair to say, is so far as the commonwealth is concerned the cradle of free trade unions. Up to this date they have never adopted this form of legislation, which is found on the North American continent where legislative bodies, in their wisdom or otherwise, have set in motion this kind of legislation for the settlement of disputes between organizations of workers and employers.
I have always felt that perhaps we are the pioneers in this kind of legislation. Only recently I read in the press statements by some of the younger leaders in labour organizations who expressed the opinion that boards of conciliation should be abolished. I believe that the form of legislation we have in Canada has done more to foster sound trade union practices than any other legislation of its kind anywhere. I am referring now of course to legislation. I believe the strength in labour legislation is to permit the people of a province or of a nation to become informed as to the facts in dispute.. The inborn common sense of the Canadian people places them in the position where it does not take them long in any labour dispute to find out who is right

and who is wrong, notwithstanding the occasional extreme opinions expressed by either side to the dispute.
If one will look over the present records of democratic countries I think he will find that the time lost last year in Canada through labour disputes was lower than that of any other country. I am speaking of course about democratic countries, and I am not including those sections which are predominantly agricultural.
I appreciate the fact, of course, that in Saskatchewan they claim to have advanced labour legislation. But there is no industry there, and their claim is pure eyewash-that is all, just pure eyewash. We are dealing with a practical thing. I believe it is fair to say that under the federal labour code the railway brotherhoods and other railway organizations, as well as other organizations coming within our jurisdiction, have functioned fairly well. And they have done so without the assistance-and I say this in a kindly way-of any governmental organization. Because it must be kept in mind that we may not always have a government like this one.
