speechtext: It being nine o'clock, the house will resume the business under consideration before recess.
The house resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott for committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few observations, very brief, on the debate which took place this afternoon. At that time the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) moved an amendment that consideration be given to the appointment of a royal commission for the purpose of-and I condense the effect of it-assisting in the improvement of government. The amendment is worded in terms which I suggest should not give offence to the most delicate temperament. It was put forward in a most cogent manner. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) referred to a similar commission, the Hoover commission, which had been appointed in the United States. He gave a good deal of evidence as to the useful work that commission had done. He referred to the fact that in the United States they had been able to command the gratuitous services of a great many citizens of standing and ability who were prepared to spend time-I presume many months-in trying to study and make observations as to how the business of government could be improved.
There are perhaps two reasons which could have been alleged as reasons for refusing to accept this amendment. The first might be that things in Canada were so good that there is no need to try to improve them at all. Anyone who heard the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), and is compos mentis, I am sure will not give that as the reason. I am sure the minister would not give it as the reason. He gave us a grave statement of our position, and I do not think "grave" is too strong a word to use. I shall not take up the time of the house in dwelling on what he said, as I think we all remember the salient features.
He told us that our expenditures had reached the colossal sum of $2,400 million and could not be reduced. Secondly, he told us that we had a surplus which really is no surplus, which really might disappear in the twinkling of an eye. Thirdly, he reminded


us that we were still riding the crest of a five-year boom, or at any rate had not come down off it. Therefore I think the first reason for not accepting the amendment of the leader of the opposition can be dismissed. I do not think anyone will suggest seriously that that reason should be accepted.
The second reason that might have been given is that nothing could be done, that no outside body could help. I think that reason is out too. It is out, first of all, on the ground of common sense. No sensible man, least of all a man like the Minister of Finance, who I think is a modest man- politics sometimes places people in the position where they have to assume an omniscience which I am sure they do not always feel-will take the position that things are so good that they cannot be improved. At any rate it is not competent, for the government to take that position because in the case of the film board they have done the very thing we are proposing. This afternoon the minister sought to distinguish between that case and what we are suggesting, but I do not think he made a very sound job of it. In fact, I think he made a very poor job. We may remind ourselves that this is no new thing. As far back as 1918 a business organization was brought in to help sort out some of the difficulties under the Civil Service Act. Some three years ago we had an eminent business organization come in. Indeed I think it is only common sense that we should be able to get help from outside.
What in fact did the minister say by way of reply? His reply disappointed me a good deal. There was an item carried in the Gazette just after he made his broadcast a couple of weeks ago which depicted the minister as being in quite a reasonable mood. But I am afraid that he has since fallen in with evil companions. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) told us this afternoon that the minister had been consorting with the cabinet and it was their view that he expressed this afternoon.
It seems to me that instead of dealing with this matter, as I think it should be dealt with, as a matter of public interest, he chose to deal with it as being entirely a matter of party. He suggested that we were not justified in setting up an outside body. He said that that was the function of the opposition. Then he went on to say that we should get down to brass tacks in the public accounts committee. Considering that that committee began to meet only yesterday, I think he was a little precipitate. Then he said, "We have the right to expect parliament to do the job that the public sends the members here to do."

Let me say to the minister, as the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) would say, in a kindly way, that for him to suggest that that could be done by members of parliament, even if we had all the brains of a Churchill or the patience of an Attlee or whatever other man you think is most patient, is unrealistic. We could not possibly give the continuous, organized attention which would be necessary.
At any rate the suggestion made in the amendment of the leader of the opposition is an entirely different thing. I propose to concentrate on this one point and not get involved in criticism of the government. The minister chose to consider this as being a critical matter, but I do not think it was intended that way. I think it was intended to be a constructive suggestion which could be taken up in a non-partisan manner. I say in passing, referring to what the minister said this afternoon, that certainly the means of giving information could be improved, but even with all the information that could be given, even with all the work that could be done, even with all the capacity that could be put into it, the best opposition in the world could not do what it is suggested in this amendment should be done. That can be done only by people with technical training, by people qualified in various ways, and above all by people who would spend a long time on the job.
Let us consider what would happen in the business world if a situation of this kind arose. Has anyone any doubt what would happen in a business concern if the general manager came to the annual meeting and said, "Our expenses are such and such and we cannot lower them; our earnings are such and such and they show a margin which is really no margin at all. We have been travelling in especially good times, but it will be the greatest of good fortune if they continue." What would happen if it were left at that? The Minister of Finance left us at that point because he gave us no lead, he gave us no suggestion of an alert and vigorous development which will provide extra income that we need.
I come back to the illustration of the company. What would the directors say to a general manager who came to them and faced them with such a forbidding prospect of deficits, and perhaps worse than deficits, unless they had unbelievable good fortune in the years immediately facing them? I suggest that what they would do would be to say, "Let us get the best brains we can to come in and look at this business. They may not be any better minds than our own,
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry but they will be fresh minds and will be able to look at things in a way we have not been able to ourselves."
If that is true of business, how much more true should it be of government, which combines many businesses and which I suppose is more intricate and difficult than any other business in the world. Why should not it be done that way? That is practically all I have to say, but before I take my seat I wish to make it very clear that I would like to think the press would make it clear to the people of this country that this amendment which is to be voted on is not to be regarded as a party or partisan amendment.
It is couched in such terms that any member of the government party could vote for it. I put it this way: Anyone who votes against it is not voting in the interests of the people of Canada which no one can deny would be served by this amendment. He will be voting against it purely because he conceives it to be in the interests of his party to do so. I should like to emphasize that. I hope earnestly that that can be brought across to the people of this country and that they will realize that if this amendment is turned down it is turned down for that reason and no other.

Mr. Speaker, theoretically I would be in favour of the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) if he had not suggested that we should have a royal commission to study some business that is our own. I do' not see why the House of Commons should call upon any judge, active or retired, to tell us what we ought to do. I have more confidence in the 261 members of parliament -excluding myself-who are my colleagues than I have in any judge, when it comes to examining our own business and deciding what we should do.
On this point I want to express my appreciation to the leader of the opposition, who understands his duties better than any of his illustrious predecessors. Those gentlemen used to agree to everything. Their business seemed to be to nod to the government every time anything came up. They were yes men, and they practised only shadow-boxing. The leader of the opposition is different. I have listened with great interest to some speeches that have been made by my colleagues of the other side to promote reform. We need reform; I am all for it.
I have had to complain many times about some civil servants, but I did my share to improve conditions. Long before the war, when Mr. Bennett was in power, he instituted a so-called economic council, which I

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry opposed. I was alone in my opposition. One of the leaders of my party stopped me when
I was arguing against that legislation, because it was a fine day and he wanted to play golf. I was really disappointed; I was carrying on my fight alone, as hon. members who were reading the newspapers at that time may remember. That legislation was piloted through by Sir George Perley, who was acting prime minister while Mr. Bennett was receiving his friends at the Chateau and was not well enough to come here. On March 18, 1935, at page 1797 of Hansard, Mr. King had this to say about the economic council: ... it was first of all proposed to be in the nature of an advisory body which would be able to assist the Prime Minister in the discharge of his onerous duties, and that it would come under the direction of the Prime Minister himself. There seemed to be the other purpose, which is that of research-a body that would be concerned primarily with research into social and economic questions- and as such would be made up of or avail itself of the services of members of the public service whose efforts and work would be supplemented by experts from outside.
Both purposes X think are not only worthy but necessary ones at the present time.
The idea was to take deputy ministers from every department and form an underground government, a kind of subgovernment that would advise the real government about everything. I waited patiently, and finally in 1936 I introduced a very short bill, 1 Edward VIII, chapter 5, which provided: Chapter nineteen of the statutes of 1935, an act to establish an economic council, is hereby repealed.
I glory in the fact that at that time I had the support of Mr. King. Before an attack there must be a bombardment; and the bill was passed on a Wednesday, after a stormy caucus in the morning. I spoke to the cabinet about the urgency of abolishing the economic council. I do not intend to read Hansard, though I have brought my personal files; and on the front page of the Ottawa Journal of February 28, 1936, at the beginning of that session, I find this:
Bill to Abolish Economic Council Passes in House
Pouliot measure is approved after Prime Minister says cabinet council satisfies him.
I remember that I was opposed by the leader of the C.C.F., who could not understand that a private member could bring in legislation to abolish something that was sacred, a conglomeration of intelligentsia. I was pretty bitter in my reply, though I had high regard for Mr. Woodsworth. He was a great man; but I wanted to pass my bill. And the Journal went on to say:
The economic council was superfluous, said Prime Minister Mackenzie King when the repealing bill was in committee.

I succeeded in changing his mind about the bureaucrats. It did not last long, but I succeeded that time.
The council was supposed to advise the Prime Minister, but as far as he was concerned he was quite satisfied with the cabinet as a council.
Mr. King's comment followed a demand from J. S Woodsworth, C.C.F. leader, for a statement from the government. He said it was unusual for a private member's bill on an important matter of policy to go through without a word from the government. Mr. Woodsworth said he believed an economic council could serve a useful purpose in Canada. There was no division.
The bill passed like that, in two or three minutes. It has been one of the glories of my parliamentary life that I have tried to curb bureaucracy; but that was only what we call a moral victory, because not long afterwards the war came. So I read in the Toronto Globe and Mail of Friday, February 5, 1943, the heading "Wide functions given to economic committee", with a picture of W. C. Clark, the deputy minister of finance. So the government went back to Bennett's practice of having an economic committee. It was not an economic council, because there was a law repealing the economic council. It came back under another name, an economic committee. Now we have scores and hundreds of these economic committees. The trouble with them is that when a man is appointed to an important position in the public service he does not do the work he is assigned to do. He tries to get together with others to do something he knows nothing about, and to travel and see the world. That is the idea. If we have people from five different departments to decide five different things,, they may be experts in their own departments but none of the five is an expert in any other department. But when they are together, they are five instead of one. They have five times more learning. We have to bow to them and say, "Oh, he is an expert; he is a civil servant". When it comes to a member of parliament he is nothing; he is a nonentity. It is extraordinary.
The leader of the opposition's motion reminds me of the motion of the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), recommending that a judge or a royal commission should study our business. He has more confidence in those people than he has in members of parliament. He does not seem to realize that when he makes such a suggestion he is discrediting himself.

Something occurred in 1937 that I should like to mention. After Mr. Bennett's defeat in the election, I spoke to Mr. Finlayson, who is now one of the officials of the Conservative party, and suggested that Mr. Bennett should take a vacation. I said to him, "He is a man of means, why does he not travel around the world? Why does he not see this planet and get away from Ottawa?" He had had a strenuous election, and I thought it would be good for him to go down to the Antipodes. Mr. Finlayson asked me whether he should tell him, and I said, "Sure, tell him; it is sincere advice from someone who has a certain degree of admiration for him."
Mr. Bennett thought it was not good for a man to be alone, and he wanted a companion to travel with him around the world. He called for Brooks from the Bank of Canada. He was well attired, well groomed, and I think he is still there. Whenever someone looks at him, they think he is a duke. They think he is the governor of the Bank of . Canada. He is a fine man. You will see, sir, that there is a relationship between what I am saying and the amendment before you. So Bennett left with Brooks, and Brooks was carrying the satchel. People were surprised. They said, "How is it that Bennett does not carry a satchel too?" They seemed to be two gentlemen. Brooks went along carrying the satchel, and in the meantime the Bank of Canada had been established. Brooks was there as the doorman. He left his important

. . . questions as to matters of internal management were not usually answered in the house unless in the judgment of the management they could be answered without affecting the day to day management of the business.

I was told that I should never ask questions like that. Mr. King rose to the occasion, and on this same page of Hansard we find the following:

The right hon. gentleman has referred to myself, when leader of the opposition, having taken with me a messenger, who was attached to the office of the leader of the opposition, when I was absent from Ottawa on one or two occasions. My right hon. friend did not say, though I imagine the omission was an inadvertent one on his part, that I personally paid all the travelling and other expenses of the messenger.
There was no question about that, but not his salary.

I paid the expenses of that messenger when I went away, and the messenger himself is a permanent official. .1 may say to my right hon. friend that he did not pay the salary of his messenger when he was absent, but the salary was paid just the same.
Quite so, when he was here.
I wonder if I could not have gone in his stead.

I will go further than that and tell the hon. gentleman that during the war, when all minds were blurred by the war, here in this house I demanded reform of the public accounts. At the time the public accounts were ridiculous. Most of the items were not in the public accounts.
I think items under $25,000 were not in the public accounts. I see present here some gentlemen who sat with me during the war. They will recall my protest to the then minister of finance. I wanted reform of the public accounts. I wanted every cent of expenditure entered in the public accounts. A measure of reform was brought about. One day one of the members for Wellington asked Mr. Ilsley df he was going to do something about that, and if he had done it upon his request. Mr. Ilsley said, "I have done so at the request of the hon. member for Temiscouata." I do not come here with large volumes of Hansard and quote excerpts from it. Hon. members who were here during the war, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) who was assistant to the then minister of finance, must remember that I demanded reform; and I am sure that I have the support of the present Minister of Finance who was assistant to the then minister whom I have quoted.
I carried on the fight to protect the Canadian people, because when there is mystery, when there is darkness, anything can be done. Crimes are not committed in the daylight; most of the time they are committed at night. I therefore wanted some light on the public accounts. I admit that the accounts are much better kept now than they were then, with regard to the officials under the jurisdiction of the minister. But when it comes to those who belong to crown companies, it is a different story. All those who belong to crown companies, to any one of them, should bow to parliament. They should be curbed. They should be told to respect parliament. That was my intention
[Mr. Pouliot.l

and it was the intention of the civil service committee in 1938 and 1939. We wanted to know what was the usefulness to the state of each civil servant. The matter was considered not from the point of view of salary, as had always been done before and as it is the intention to do in the future. The usefulness of each man was to be considered. That was our point of view. After some difficulty we succeeded in presenting a unanimous report. Unfortunately, it was of no use because the prime minister of the time did not realize that the civil service committee was offering him, on a silver platter, the full control of the civil service of Ottawa. It was offered twice, the first time by me on behalf of the committee, and the second time by the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier), also on behalf of the committee; and both times it was left on the shelf to gather dust. We wanted reform. I want reform.
I am not going to take the time of the house to read what I quoted in the house in Hansard of May 26, 1939, on the Central Mortgage bank bill; but it is there. I mentioned some interesting historical Canadian papers, especially the 92 resolutions about the management and control of public affairs.
I disagree wholeheartedly with my friends of the C.C.F. group when they speak of control. They speak of control outside parliament. All control should be vested in parliament and parliament has not the right to delegate it to anyone. When any hon. member is elected, he is elected in the first place to look after the interests of the Canadian people. He is elected to look after not only the people of his constituency but the Canadian people at large, by enacting legislation that may affect every man, woman and child in this country.
I may add that we also have an important duty and that is to check the expenditure of the public money voted in the house. Both duties are most important. In fact, they are the main duties of members of parliament.
It is our duty to pass legislation and to check the expenditure of money. I do not see what business a judge has in it.
I will bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, and to that of hon. members of the house, . an important paper passed at Westminster with regard to the control of expenditure.
It was passed at the request of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's treasury. There is a council of financial officers, and it is the interim report on the position of accounting officers. It is dated March 12, 1920. At the time I distributed a copy of this paper to all my colleagues in the house, and this is the last copy I have. It reads as follows:

Council of financial officers
Interim report on the position of accounting officers
At their first meeting the council proceeded to discuss the general position of accounting officers and the possibility of effecting reform in the present financial procedure of departments. On the 10th November, 1919, the Chancellor of the Exchequer requested the council to consider, together with other proposals for strengthening the hands of accounting officers, the suggestion contained in paragraph 9 of the first report of the select committee on national expenditure (1919), that the accounting officer of each spending department should be a treasury official appointed by and solely responsible to the treasury.
9. The proposal that the accounting officer shall be a treasury official does not commend itself to us.
(i.) In the first place, it offends against the cardinal principle of ministerial responsibility. A minister could not be properly responsible to parliament for the conduct of his department if a large part of the responsibility falls actually on the servant of another department to whom he *is unable to give orders.
(ii.) In the second place, the tendency to evade financial control alluded to above should, in our view, become more marked if the officer to be evaded were an emissary of another department.
At the present the financial officer is the servant of the same minister as the administrative officers, and is entitled to the same access to official papers and confidential information as they are; these are advantages of great value in financial control which might be lost if he became an officer of the treasury.
(iii.) Thirdly, the treasury officer could not work single-handed. He would require staff. This would presumably have to be treasury staff, too. There would thus be an elaborate interviewing of the staff of two departments under one roof, under conditions which would almost inevitably give rise to friction and discontent.
(iv.) The position obtaining in the ministry of transport does not afford a precedent for the proposal that the accounting officer should be a treasury official. The accounting officer of the ministry of transport is responsible to the minister, but works in close association with a treasury officer specially attached to the ministry in view of peculiar circumstances arising out of the ministry of transport act.
Those principles were enunciated with regard to one department, but they apply to all, and this is true British doctrine.
This afternoon I listened with a great deal of interest to the splendid speech made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). He mentioned to us the example of the United States. We may learn a lot from any country, but I still stand on the British parliamentary practice, on the British parliamentary tradition, which is the best in the world. I do not mean some silly rulings of Speakers of past centuries. Naturally an understanding of British traditions should be in accordance with our time; but there in that treasury of British parliamentary traditions we can find principles that may serve for the guidance of all parliaments.
I cannot speak too highly of those who have been acting in accordance with that tradition, and my hope in this parliament is that it

Coming to the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), I will tell him once more that in some respects I agree with him, because I suffer a great deal from having to telephone to this gentleman, to telephone to that other gentleman, to be sent back to a third gentleman, and by that gentleman to be sent to a fourth lady. There is no need for it; and there is no answer. My files pile up. If I am not always in the house listening to speeches and making an occasional one, it is just because my time is taken up with that correspondence. I have not been elected to be a scribe. I have been elected to read legislation and to try my best to understand it; to discuss it with my colleagues; and to attend to committees. I have never been a public stenographer. At the present time I have to spend my time on the telephone, writing letters and most of the time getting no satisfactory answers. Things are delayed from one day to the other. We have to look after that. It is not sensible at all. I say nothing of myself, because I am full of modesty, when I telephone to those great of the world. It is a pretty tough life.

I appreciate the fact that the leader of the opposition has moved an amendment. It has been discussed, and it is a good thing. But I am a Liberal and supporter of the present government, and especially of my leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I have confidence in him, and I sincerely believe that in the next three or four years he can do a better job in matters of reform than the leader of the opposition can do, although the latter made many useful suggestions. Therefore I will vote against the amendment, although I have been challenged by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell). I will vote against it for two reasons. The main reason is that I do not want a judge to be appointed to do what we should do ourselves, and what I have started to do in my humble and minor capacity. It is evident that all the members together could do a better job than I have done alone. Hon. members could do that. The leader of the opposition might be surprised at the sympathy and support that he would get even from Liberals in that connection.
In the first place, I am opposed to a judge looking after our own business; and in the second place, I rely on my leader to carry out all the possible reforms that he believes should be carried out while he himself is in office. The difficulty in reforms is that all temporary employees want to be permanent. The leader of the opposition, who has been premier of his province, must know that better than any one of us. It is most difficult to abolish any position, because then people come along and say that the position is


essential, that there has been no better incumbent, that the man is qualified, and so on. I have heard that many times; everybody has heard it. I am reminded of the case of the girl who was in the civil service at the time of the civil service probe twelve years ago. Her first name was Dorothy, and I shall not give her family name. Dorothy had missed her examination nine times. I said to Mr. Nelson, the civil service commissioner, who was a very fine man, "Mr. Nelson, you should fire her." He said, "I will." Two days after that he called me by telephone and said, "Do you know who has protested on behalf of Miss Dorothy?" I said, "No." He said, "Her chief. He found that she was doing essential work in the office." I do not know what her work was, nor do I know her qualifications, because I never met her. But as soon as she was fired her chief protested to the civil service commission and said she was indispensable.
That is one illustration of what I have been saying. I do not wish to be unfair to the leader of the opposition or to anyone else. But this is the time to read to the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Drew) and other hon. members an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal.

The Ottawa Journal of Friday, October 15, 1948, carries an editorial which bears the heading, "Mr. Drew and the Bureaucrats". It states:
What is all this silly talk about Mr. Drew planning, when he takes office, to fire Graham Towers, Donald Gordon, Dr. Clifford Clark, Louis Rasminsky, and Dr. Kenneth Taylor?
Mr. Drew, in the speech which has given rise to such nonsense, said nothing about firing anybody.
Nothing about Dorothy!
What he said, and quite properly, was that if he became prime minister he would make an end of ruch things as taxes imposed by radio, and that policies would be decided not by a few officials but by the cabinet and parliament. Mr. Drew, saying this, was paraphrasing a plank in his party's platform:
"The Progressive Conservative party reiterates its belief in the supremacy of parliament and is opposed to the increasing use of ministerial proclamation and government by order in council and departmental regulations."
Nothing revolutionary in that. Indeed, we imagine that Messrs. Towers, Gordon and Clark would be among the first to subscribe to it. For it is our belief that these gentlemen, to the extent that they have been running this country, have been the products and victims of a weak cabinet and parliament. They have not been asked to work out policies decided by the cabinet and parliament; they have been asked to tell the cabinet and parliament what policies should be adopted. That happens when parliament and the cabinet are incompetent.
We ourselves think that Messrs. Towers, Gordon and Clark are the sort of officials who would get on famously with Mr. Drew; that they are the sort of able officials he would like to have at his elbow, and he the sort of decisive prime minister they would like to serve.
Incidentally, the Bank of Canada, with its Governor Towers and Deputy Governor Gordon, is not the creature of Mr. King nor of a Liberal government. The Bank of Canada was set up by Mr. Bennett, with Mr. Graham Towers his choice for its first governor.
I wonder if the leader of the opposition could make any one of the reforms he has suggested?
I thank you, sir, and I thank the house for having permitted me to read this fine editorial.

1. Reducing public expenditure to the lowest point consistent with efficiency.
It is my understanding that in appointing a royal commission the terms of reference must be well defined. They must be sharp, and cover some definite subject. This term of reference is extremely broad, that of reducing public expenditure to the lowest point consistent with efficiency. Who is going to decide whether or not expenditures are consistent with efficiency? Is it to be this parliament or the one-man, two-man, or three-man royal commission? That seems to me to be a fatal flaw in the amendment which would prevent any person who considers it free from party considerations supporting it.
We come now to the next two proposals, which read:
Eliminating duplication of overlapping services.
Consolidating all public services and departmental activities of a similar nature.
It seems to me that that is not the function of a royal commission. In my opinion that would be the function of expert business managers. My knowledge of royal commissions is that they usually engage in eliciting facts and on the basis of those facts make recommendations, but they are not recommendations such as would be required in the circumstances set out in the two terms of reference in the amendment. Then we come to the last proposal, which reads:
Improving the general efficiency of government and assuring to all members of the civil service full recognition of their responsibilities.
Can anyone tell me how a royal commission could perform that function or could make recommendations by which those things could be carried out? These are the reasons why in my opinion no one who examines carefully the terms of this amendment can vote for it. I quite agree with the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) and some other members who have spoken on this amendment that what is being asked here to be done by a royal commission is something that should be and must be done by parliament itself if hon. members are to take their responsibilities seriously.

That applies just as much to members on the government side as it does to members of the opposition. True it is that the function of an opposition is to watch government administration, to draw attention to weaknesses in it, to draw attention to unnecessary or unwise expenditures; but because of the operations of chance the government majority at the present time is so large that a tremendous responsibility rests, not only upon the ministers but upon the private members on the government side. A minister should be the first to be pleased when an hon. member of his party examines carefully what that government is doing.
The hon. member for Greenwood says that those of us who vote against this amendment will be doing so because we are voting in the interests of our parties. I would put it the other way and say that anyone who votes for this amendment in the terms in which it is stated is forgetting the interests of the country and perhaps the functions of parliament and is thinking in terms of the interests of his party.
For these reasons we shall have to vote against the amendment although, as I have said before, we agree with much of what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) and other members of the official opposition have said when speaking to the amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I listened this afternoon with a great deal of interest to the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). However, I think if we disrobe his declarations of their glamorous vestments we will find that the bare subject is quite lean. His proposal for a royal commission rests on two assumptions. First, that the executive machinery of the government must be geared perfectly to the expanded functions it is called upon to perform. Second, that parliament may need new and better methods of controlling the advisability of voting certain estimates and of scrutinizing the way in which appropriations have been spent.
It may very well be that all is not perfect in all departments of government. It may very well be that the Hoover commission performed a valuable work in the United States. But I doubt if anyone will suggest that the functions of government in Canada have been enlarged in any comparable way in the last ten years with those in the United States. True there has been a considerable change since the days when we operated the government services on $200 million a year, but it still is possible for the government machinery to be surveyed and checked by the means we have at hand without having recourse to outsiders.
[Mr. Maclnnis.l
The treasury board, the comptroller of the treasury, the civil service commission and the auditor general's office keep a constant eye on the evolution of our services and.serve as a salutary check on undue expansion of expenditures and avoidable duplications.
As far as the house is concerned, there is no limitation to its right of inquiry. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) stated, hon. members have used that right with ability and should not suddenly turn into humble violets or suffer from an inferiority complex and ask that their powers be turned over to others. Parliamentary machinery exists whereby members of this house may scrutinize the estimates and the way in which appropriations have been spent.
I do not say that there could not be a better use made of this machinery, but I know of no impediment that would prevent hon. members from grilling one or all of the ministers on any item in their estimates which the opposition might suspect was extravagant or unjustified. I know of no impediment in the way of members of the opposition or of any other group or of the government bringing to the attention of the public accounts committee any irregularity or any abuse that they think might exist. I shall deal with the work of that committee further on in my remarks.
The examples given this afternoon by the leader of the opposition to substantiate his charges that inefficiency or duplication of services exists were certainly very poorly chosen. To hinge the urgency for a royal commission on the fact that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) had fifty-six persons on his publicity staff and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) thirty-eight, and to invoke the alleged photographic war between those departments, hardly substantiates the urgency that exists, according to the leader of the opposition, of summoning a body of experts to decide whether twenty people would not suffice to draft the illustrated information which the two departments feel it advisable to distribute.
I do not intend, nor have I a brief, to speak for the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Minister of National Defence; but anyone acquainted with the publications of the Department of National Health and Welfare will realize their high standards and their considerable value to the people of Canada. I do not think any sarcastic remarks can take away from the merit of the minister in having given an impetus and vitality to all the services of his department for the benefit of our people and the benefit of the national health. When I consider the

conditions in the world today and the necessarily high cost of military protection, 1 do not find the publicity estimates of that department extravagant, either. I have no doubt the Minister of National Defence will be able to answer any questions the opposition may have to ask on the matter when his estimates are before the house.
So I say that if the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) could not find anything better to which to devote a considerable portion of his time, or if he could not bring before us facts more startling or arguments more striking, there is very little justification for the motion. We sit here for months every year. We are in constant contact with departmental activities. Surely if things were so bad members of the opposition would have discovered that fact and acquainted the house with their discoveries. That there may be room for improvement in departmental administration I would be the last to deny. This is the case with every great enterprise; and when that enterprise has to be run on democratic principles many elements enter into it which may necessitate a constant survey lest the machinery become cumbersome and inefficient. Yet I know of few organizations more open to scrutiny and control than our federal administration. The departmental administrators live in glass houses, and it is not hard for members of this house to peep in.
This afternoon the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) made certain statements which did not seem to me consistent with the facts. I am sure he never intended to give the house a wrong impression; but he said-and I took note of his exact words-that the public accounts of Canada reported only expenditures of $10,000 or more. I think that is a misleading statement, though as I say I do not believe the hon. member did it on purpose to misrepresent the situation. If you look at the public accounts, at the end of the report of each department there is a list of the amounts that have been paid to certain suppliers. That is almost always the way these lists are headed, "Suppliers receiving $10,000 or more from this department." Look at the public accounts; look at the Department of Agriculture, at page A-61. There you see a list of suppliers receiving $10,000 or more from that department, but that is not all. Immediately under that long list, in small print you see, "Payments to contractors on public works contracts, including payments for rental of equipment, of $5,000 or over are described in detail under the relevant votes and are therefore not included in the following list." In other words each amount that needs
Public Service-Proposed Inquiry governmental approval is listed elsewhere in the report, just as each salary, no matter how small, is listed.
I could say the 'same about nearly every department. At page F-24 the same information is given with respect to the wheat board, and it is indicated that these lists are exclusive of amounts of $5,000 and over. At page F-25 you find a whole list of wheat board payments totalling $5,000 or more, in respect of their activities. I am sure the house would not want this volume to contain such items as those read this afternoon by the hon. member for Lake Centre from the public accounts of 1890, covering a corkscrew and a few glasses. I do not imagine even the hon. member would want that sort of thing carried forward into the public accounts today; his statement is somewhat misleading taken in its context.
I could take a great deal of the time of this house going into every department; but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the situation I have mentioned applies in all departments. There is a list of accounts of $10,000 or more, and in addition those for more than $5,000 are reported under the heading of the vote itself. I thought that statement by the hon. member needed to be corrected, because if it were read by someone who did not know the practice of the house he might be led to believe that we considered any amount under $10,000 too small to be recorded, while actually we go down as low as $5,000. Personally, with the cost of everything a department may need as high as it is, I think $5,000 is too small an amount, and that governmental authority should be required only for projects costing $10,000 or more. However, it is the practice to report everything from $5,000 up, and each small item of salary is also shown in the public accounts.
Now I come to the statement that has been made on many occasions that the public accounts committee could do more to check the way votes approved by the house have been used by the executive branch of the administration. I am all the more interested because I have been chairman of the public accounts committee since 1945. That greater or better use of the committee could be made to scrutinize public expenditures I readily admit; but the machinery exists, and it has brought results and can bring more if the house desires. There is no rule of this house governing the time during which standing committees shall sit. The onl. provision is in connection with the special committee to draw up the membership of the other committees, and in that connection section (1) of standing order 63 provides:
At the commencement of each session, a special committee, consisting of five members, shall be

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry appointed, whose duty it shall be to prepare and report, with all convenient speed, lists of members to compose the following committees of the house-
Then follows a list of those standing committees. Standing orders 64 to 67 also deal with committees; but nowhere is there mention of any period during the session when these committees should assemble or should be asked to sit. A committee sits when certain duties have been entrusted to it by the house. The committee on banking, for instance, sits when a bill is referred to it. As for the public accounts committee, it has been the custom to refer to it, some time after the address is voted, the public accounts and the report of the Auditor General. This is not done automatically or on any given date, however. For many years the practice has been to refer the public accounts when a request to that effect has been made in the house. Once the public accounts are referred to the committee there is no special time when it must sit. The tradition has developed that the committee assembles when an hon. member signifies to the chairman-elect his desire that it should do so. In the last twenty-one years the committee has sat six times, of which four were under my chairmanship. This means that during fifteen sessions no member has availed himself of the privilege of asking that the public accounts be referred to the committee.
Will the hon. member permit a question? He said six times, when I think he meant six sessions.

I meant six sessions out of twenty-one sessions. I think that was understood by the members.
Of the four sessions during which I have presided over the committee, I must say that the utmost liberty has been given to the members to bring any subject to the attention of the committee. Yet the committee has never been asked by the opposition to examine any one item in particular in the public accounts. We have usually dealt with general considerations, and an over-all review of the Auditor General's report, as well as the work the committee might be called upon to perform. The only exception to this was in 1947, when the house referred specific questions to the committee, namely, the advisability of investigating the claims made by the Japanese evacuees. As a result of our consideration of that subject a commissioner was appointed to advise the government on those claims.
The committee was also asked to review the administration of the custodian of enemy property, and the administration of the building program of the Department of Veterans Affairs. A moment ago I stated the result of

our deliberations so far as the Japanese question was concerned, and our investigations into the veterans affairs department resulted in the removal and transfer from office of an officer about whom the committee had expressed dissatisfaction. That was the work accomplished by the committee during one parliamentary session. However, the fact that the opposition has not found cause to ask the committee to look into any item of public accounts does not necessarily mean th'at all is well. But it certainly means that there are no such unsatisfactory conditions as some members opposite pretend exist, because I have no doubt that any important irregularities would have to come to the ear of members opposite, or at least some suspicion of them would have been brought to their attention. Then they would have been brought by them to the attention of the committee. I would not for one moment think that, such being the case, the fact that they were not brought up reflected upon the ability of opposition members; far from that.
That consideration should be given to the use of the public accounts committee to scrutinize and investigate public expenditures in a more consistent manner, I agree. I do not see any objection to it. The first task of the opposition is to watch the administration, and serve as a check on any irregularity which might occur. It remains the duty of the whole house to scrutinize public expenditure. This year the committee has already had three meetings. It has before it for consideration all the public accounts and the Auditor General's report, yet its deliberations have centred more on that question of redefining its task, or of remodelling its machinery in order to better perform its functions. Some members have remarked to me that the committee was not charged with the study of the whole question of the control of public money; that is true, but the duty of that committee is to consider public accounts, and I assume it is therefore in order for it to consider how best it can perform its task. That other points may be brought in evidence given before the committee, and that they may be discussed in the committee when they are related to the study of public accounts, is unavoidable.
It will rest upon the committee to arrive at conclusions as to how it can best perform its duties this year, and in future years, and to so report to the house within the limits of its reference. Be that as it may, I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that we lack at present the machinery for surveying public expenditures by this house, and I am satisfied that precautionary measures taken by the Auditor General's office, by the treasury board and the comptroller of the treasury, as well as by the

civil service commission, are such that, coupled with the vigilance of this house, they are sufficient for protection against abuse. I think it would be an unwarranted admission of inferiority on the part of parliament to call in the so-called experts, when we have within our own rules the facilities to perform these duties.
Without desiring to be offensive, I must say the attitude of the leader of the opposition appears to be a reversal of the attitude he has adopted on more occasions than one. I still have in my ears the echo of his declaration about the supremacy of parliament. Yet today he comes here asking parliament to proclaim that it cannot perform its tasks, and that it must seek help from outsiders. The people of Canada will have a hard time reconciling the two attitudes.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think this house is not justified in adopting the motion under consideration. If this house was to approve a proposal of that kind, I think the leader of the opposition and his lieutenants would have had to build their case more strongly, and base their conclusions on safer ground. Parliament has all the machinery it needs to perform its tasks. It has done so over the past fifteen years without the help of the so-called experts from outside, and the country has never been better administered.

I am
interested in the concern of the last speaker over royal commissions, especially when one remembers that this government has not only the Massey commission, but the two other royal commissions which have recently been sitting, including the transportation commission. I think perhaps the objection to this suggestion is in the nature either of a straw man or of wishing not to have the facts of the case fully disclosed to the house. The criticism of the motion, Mr. Speaker, has been based almost entirely on ignorance of the facts.
First of all, a royal commission such as is envisaged by this resolution does not, and cannot, usurp the executive functions or powers of government. With regard to the expenditure of money, the responsibility is not the government's, it is the responsibility of this parliament. Such is the overwhelming feeling of omnipotence in the government benches that they almost invariably forget this fundamental fact of our British democratic system of parliamentary government. The adoption of this motion, Mr. Speaker, does not mean that we are taking away anything, nor is there any suggestion that we intend to take away any of the executive responsibilities of the members of the cabinet;

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry that is far from the purpose of the resolution. The resolution merely does this. It testifies and shows that parliament is supreme. Any suggestion that it does not do that is entirely in error. What the resolution tends to do is merely to show that the expenditure of money voted by parliament for the essential services of the country is efficient and expedient. That is the sum total of the import of the resolution. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that that is an important thing. With the growth of all democratic governments throughout the world, the machinery to check and to go into expenditures which was evolved in the old days, when the cost of government ran at a figure of about 5 per cent, or certainly less than 10 per cent, of the gross national income of the country, was probably satisfactory. Now, however, with the gross expenditure of government in Canada probably in excess of 25 per cent of the gross national income, new and more scientific and efficient methods must be taken to check and to go into the methods of that expenditure. This was the intent of the Hoover commission. This is the identical intent of the resolution which is today before the house. Instead of taking away from the responsibility of members of the cabinet and of this parliament, it increases the responsibility of this parliament; it tends to make the functioning of government more efficient. That is the purport of this resolution.
In his budget speech the minister said that the minimum expenditure of Canada in the foreseeable future was, let us say in round figures, two and a half billion dollars. With the increased responsibility which we may have for national defence; with the increase of pressure for expansion of the social services; with the continual pressure for increasing government services all along the line; with the added deficits of the Canadian National Railways, of Trans-Canada Air Lines and of the Canadian National Steamships; with all the other multitudinous expenditures or expenses of government, it means one thing, Mr. Speaker. Taxes can do only one thing and that is go up.
There are two ways in which we can prevent this occurrence. We can deny our responsibilities for national defence. We can retrench in the essential services. We could possibly decrease the essential services. But, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that none of these things is in keeping either with our responsibilities as an international power or with our responsibilities as a free and democratic country.
There is only one other way in which taxes may be reduced, and that is by the efficient

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry expenditure of the money voted by this parliament. The resolution before this parliament today dims at bringing about just that thing. I suggest that it is the only method by which we may ever expect to see taxes reduced from their present level. The. report of the Hoover commission, which was-trying to do exactly the same thing, showed that a reduction of $4 billion in the United States was entirely possible without any reduction in the efficiency of the government services. In fact, it showed case after case where the efficiency could be increased. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make one or two quotations from this report. They are of a general nature, and I am satisfied that if a similar commission investigated the Canadian expenditures, a similar situation would be found. This is the sort of thing that the Hoover commission discovered in the general administration of the United States. I will just quote a few of them. There are hundreds liere that I could give examples of but I will just quote a few. According to the report this is what happened. The bureau of Indian affairs employs one person for each thirty-two of the 393,000 Indians under its care. The veterans administration takes five times as long to settle insurance claims as private companies do, and uses four times the manpower per policy. The government owns three and one-half typewriters for each employee using its machines. After dismantling a $16 million camp in Alaska the army shipped the lumber to Seattle. The Department of the Interior took over the lumber and shipped it back to a point ten miles from where it originally stood.
There is so much duplication in the Department of Agriculture that a farmer received conflicting advice about fertilizers from five different units of that department. To prevent the flooding of Cherry creek, a small stream east of Denver, the army engineers tore down a dam which local engineers considered adequate and built a $15 million dam three miles long and 140 feet high. Some government bureaux are stocked with supplies fifty years in advance. The government owns $27 million of supplies and materials. There is no central inventory of this vast property. Federal jobs are so frustrating that 50,000 persons quit the government each year; yet it takes months to secure the resignation of unsatisfactory employees. Hence the Dorothy story.
Let us take an example of the Canadian administration, about which I know a little bit. Let me refer to the old department of mines and resources. For years the leading spokesmen in the mining industry have pleaded with the government to reorganize the department. They have pleaded with


the government to take out immigration and other non-mining subjects. Today the government has split that department into three, but as yet we have no minister of mines specifically responsible to that great industry. I understand today that the ministry and the department are still in 26 different buildings around Ottawa, and I presume the filing system is such that a boy on a bicycle is still the means of drawing files from a number of different central registers. When I make that criticism of the department of mines I do it, Mr. Speaker, from occasional visits and complaints of mining engineers, friends of mine, who have been frustrated despite the very excellent work being done by the engineers, the scientists and the other personnel in that department. Mind you, it is no criticism of the personnel in the department of mines; for when I make that criticism I, as a member of the opposition, make the criticism, and it is put down as political criticism; but if somebody like Dr. Camsell, with an intimate knowledge of this country and an intimate knowledge of that department, as a member of a royal commission such as is suggested, made criticism and made suggestions nobody could accuse him of any political bias. In my opinion he would be one man at least who would be extremely competent and able to suggest the reforms which I believe, and which associates of mine believe, and which many members of the mining industry believe are necessary in that one department.
We go along to all the other departments of government. I may make criticisms; I may ask questions in the public accounts committee, Mr. Speaker. I have just come 'from a committee that sat four hours on Monday, six hours I think it was on Tuesday, four hours on Wednesday, seven hours on Thursday and very nearly eight hours on Friday dealing with the unmentionable subject of pipe lines. We are told that bloody Mary, the Queen of England, said that when she died she would have "Calais" written on her heart. If I am found dead in my bunk tonight on the train to Toronto I shall have "pipe lines" written around my viscera.
Mary, Queen of Scots.

No, bloody Mary; not Mary, Queen of Scots: she had her head cut off. I am right in my queen. With all due respect, the question of investigating parliamentary expenditures through the committee system is archaic at the present time. Anybody who will take the trouble to read the reports of the committee going into the expenditures of the Canadian National Railways will see that. Before that committee we had as witness Mr. Donald Gordon and his experts, who

gave a very able presentation of their problem. The plain fact is that today government has got beyond the committee stage. We have got beyond the public accounts committee stage. This parliament is by far the biggest spender of money in the country. No business, no private individual, could possibly remain solvent using the" methods this parliament uses to control expenditures.
I want to say one thing about pressure groups. Today in all democratic countries every member, every freely elected member, is subject to pressure groups. There was one here recently. The recent mail that hon. members have been getting with regard to the means test, the various groups in the country who are organized for special interests, are all capable of exerting political pressure at times of election on members of this House of Commons and to any freely elected legislature.
It is human for a candidate to want to be elected; it is human for a candidate, by promise or by the soft answer, to, shall we say, not turn away wrath but to take perhaps a less direct line than the facts cf the case indicate. And that pressure is evidenced in the debates in this house, it is evidenced in discussions in committee, and it is evidenced generally through the behaviour of all freely elected parliaments.
Now, were a royal commission, a nonpolitical royal commission such as the group under Mr. Hoover in the United States, to bring down a report such as has been brought down in the United States, a very different attitude might be taken, and a much more realistic attitude, for the welfare of the entire country.
I say this to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), that one of the most striking bits of evidence at the present time in the United States is that members of the congress returning to Washington almost unanimously report that the question uppermost in the minds of their constituents at home is the expenditure by the federal government. The

Public Service-Proposed Inquiry Hoover report has taken the place of the cold war, has taken the place of the Taft-Hartley Act, has taken the place of all the other contentious items, in the opinions of members of the congress who are returning to Washington.
That is a most salutary thing to happen. Unless and until the full implication of the total mass government expenditure and its effect on the lives of every citizen of the country is fully realized, we are heading for increased expenditures and increased taxation until such time-and that time will come-that the total national expenditures of government reach a percentage point of the total national income from which a recovery to individual freedom will be impossible. What that point is may be debatable. It is certainly less than 35 per cent, and it is possibly more than 25 per cent. But today the expenditures of government in Canada are above the 25 per cent mark. This transcends, I believe, every economic and security issue in Canada today.
Efficiency must be restored and must be brought to big government. We have seen that the methods we already have at our disposal cannot and do not bring about that efficiency. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I support the amendment moved by my leader, the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Drew). It is a case of whether we are going to be defeated by bankruptcy or whether we are prepared to fight for our own individual freedom as free men in this country.
On motion of Mr. Ross (Souris) the debate was adjourned.
